goals: State the properties of a genetic material
Describe the experiments of Griffith, Avery–MacLeod–McCarty and Hershey–Chase
Describe the double helix and the contributions of Miescher, Chargaff, Wilkins, Franklin, Watson and Crick
Compare DNA and RNA, name the types of RNA, and describe DNA packaging

slides.heading: Molecular Basis of Inheritance
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what the genetic material is, how it was found, and how it is built and packed.

visual.alt: Flow from Mendel’s factors to chromosomes to DNA

slides.narration: Mendel’s factors were placed on chromosomes, but which molecule in chromosomes carries inheritance? Chromosomes contain both protein and nucleic acid. A series of elegant experiments showed that the genetic material is deoxyribonucleic acid, DNA, and in some viruses ribonucleic acid, RNA.

slides.heading: What makes a good genetic material?
slides.body_md: A molecule that acts as genetic material must meet four criteria.

rows: Complementary base pairing allows exact copying
DNA lacks the reactive 2′-OH of RNA and has thymine, so it is more stable
Base changes are rare but possible

visual.alt: Table of the four criteria of a genetic material

slides.narration: Both DNA and RNA can replicate and mutate, but RNA is more reactive and less stable. That is why DNA is the predominant genetic material, while RNA, which can also act as a catalyst, is thought to have been the first genetic material.

slides.heading: Griffith: transformation

slides.narration: Something from the dead smooth bacteria changed the harmless rough bacteria into the deadly form. Griffith called it the transforming principle, but he could not say what it was. That question was answered by later biochemical work.

slides.heading: Avery, MacLeod and McCarty
slides.body_md: Working between **1933 and 1944**, **Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod and Maclyn McCarty** purified biochemicals (proteins, DNA, RNA) from heat-killed S cells to find which one transformed R cells.

visual.alt: Table of enzyme treatments and transformation results

slides.narration: Only purified DNA caused transformation, and only the DNA-digesting enzyme stopped it. They concluded that DNA is the hereditary material, though not all biologists were convinced until the phage experiments that followed.

slides.heading: Hershey and Chase
slides.body_md: In **1952**, **Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase** grew bacteriophages with radioactive **phosphorus (³²P)**, which labels DNA, or radioactive **sulphur (³⁵S)**, which labels protein. After infection, blending and centrifugation, **³²P** was found **inside the bacteria** and **³⁵S** outside.

slides.heading: Discovering the double helix
slides.body_md: Several scientists contributed to the model.

rows: Isolated an acidic substance, “nuclein”, from the nuclei of pus cells
In double-stranded DNA, A = T and G = C, so purines = pyrimidines
X-ray diffraction data on DNA structure
Double helix model with complementary base pairing

visual.alt: Table of scientists and their contributions to DNA structure

slides.narration: Miescher first isolated DNA in 1869, but its structure took almost a century to solve. Chargaff’s base ratios and Franklin and Wilkins’s X-ray images were the clues Watson and Crick used to build their model in 1953.

slides.heading: The double helix
slides.body_md: Two **polynucleotide chains** form a **right-handed** helix with a **sugar–phosphate backbone** outside and **bases** inside. The chains are **antiparallel** (5′→3′ and 3′→5′). **A pairs with T** (two hydrogen bonds) and **G with C** (three). The pitch is **3.4 nm**, with about **10 base pairs per turn**, so bases are **0.34 nm** apart.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: Chargaff’s rules
slides.body_md: A double-stranded DNA sample has 20 percent adenine. Find the percentages of the other bases. Write the complementary strand of 5′–ATGCCGTA–3′.
bullets: $T = A = 20$ percent.
Complementary strand (3′→5′): **TACGGCAT**.

visual.alt: Worked table: A and T 20, G and C 30 percent

slides.narration: Adenine equals thymine, so both are twenty percent. That leaves sixty percent for guanine and cytosine together, thirty each. To write the partner strand, pair each base with its complement and remember the partner runs in the opposite direction.

slides.heading: DNA, RNA and the three kinds of RNA
slides.body_md: DNA and RNA are both polynucleotides but differ in sugar, bases and form.

rows: mRNA (template), tRNA (adapter carrying amino acids), rRNA (structural and catalytic in ribosomes)

visual.alt: Table comparing DNA and RNA and listing types of RNA

slides.narration: Messenger RNA carries the code from DNA to the ribosome. Transfer RNA reads the code and brings the right amino acid. Ribosomal RNA forms part of the ribosome and catalyses the joining of amino acids.

slides.heading: Packaging DNA: nucleosomes
slides.body_md: In eukaryotes, positively charged basic proteins, **histones** (rich in lysine and arginine), form an **octamer**. Negatively charged DNA wraps around it to form a **nucleosome** of about **200 bp**. Nucleosomes appear as **beads on a string**; the chromatin fibre is coiled further into chromosomes, helped by **non-histone chromosomal proteins**.

goals: State the central dogma and explain reverse transcription

slides.heading: Central dogma and replication
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how genetic information flows and how DNA copies itself.

visual.alt: Flow of the central dogma: DNA replicates and is transcribed to RNA, which is translated to protein

slides.narration: Francis Crick proposed the central dogma: genetic information flows from DNA to RNA to protein. DNA copies itself by replication, its information is transcribed into RNA, and RNA is translated into protein.

slides.heading: Reverse transcription
slides.body_md: In some viruses, such as **retroviruses** (for example **HIV**), information flows **from RNA to DNA**. The enzyme **reverse transcriptase** makes DNA from the viral RNA, an exception to the original direction of the central dogma.

visual.alt: Flow of reverse transcription in a retrovirus

slides.narration: Reverse transcription lets a retrovirus insert its genes into the host’s chromosomes, where they are copied with the host’s own DNA. The discovery showed that information can sometimes flow backwards from RNA to DNA.

slides.heading: Quick check: reverse transcription
slides.body_md: Which enzyme copies RNA into DNA?
slides.narration: Quick check. Its name says that it reverses transcription.

slides.heading: Semi-conservative replication
slides.body_md: Watson and Crick proposed that the two strands **separate** and each acts as a **template** for a new complementary strand. Each daughter molecule has **one parental and one new strand**: **semi-conservative replication**.

rows: Each has one old and one new strand
One wholly old, one wholly new
Old and new pieces mixed in each strand

visual.alt: Table of three models of DNA replication

slides.narration: Only the semi-conservative model fits the experiments. Because each strand serves as a template, the two daughter molecules are identical to each other and to the parent.

slides.heading: Meselson and Stahl (1958)
slides.body_md: **E. coli** were grown for many generations in **¹⁵NH₄Cl**, so their DNA became **heavy**, then transferred to **¹⁴NH₄Cl**. DNA was separated by **caesium chloride density-gradient centrifugation**. After one generation (about 20 minutes) all DNA was **hybrid**; after two generations (40 minutes) **half hybrid and half light**.

slides.body_md: Following Meselson and Stahl, what fractions of the DNA will be heavy, hybrid and light after three generations in ¹⁴N?
bullets: After $n$ generations, only the 2 original strands remain, in 2 hybrid molecules out of $2^{n}$.

slides.heading: Taylor’s experiment
slides.body_md: In **1958**, **J. H. Taylor** grew root tips of **Vicia faba** (broad bean) in medium with **radioactive thymidine** for one generation, then in non-radioactive medium, and located the label by **autoradiography**.

rows: After one division in labelled medium
Both chromatids of each chromosome labelled
After a further division in unlabelled medium
Only one chromatid of each chromosome labelled

visual.alt: Table of Taylor’s observations with labelled thymidine

slides.narration: Taylor showed that chromosomes of a plant, not only bacterial DNA, replicate semi-conservatively. Each chromatid keeps one old strand and makes one new strand, so the label is shared out exactly as the model predicts.

slides.heading: The machinery of replication
slides.body_md: Replication starts at an **origin of replication**. At the **replication fork**, the strands unwind. **DNA-dependent DNA polymerase** adds nucleotides only in the **5′→3′** direction, so the **leading strand** is made **continuously** and the **lagging strand** **discontinuously** as **Okazaki fragments**, joined by **DNA ligase**.

notes.title: Molecular Basis of Inheritance: DNA and Replication — Notes

sections.heading: 1. The search for the genetic material
sections.body_md:
**Properties of a genetic material:** it should (i) be able to generate its own replica; (ii) be stable chemically and structurally; (iii) provide scope for slow changes (mutation) required for evolution; (iv) be able to express itself as Mendelian characters. DNA meets these better than RNA: the **2′-OH** of ribose makes RNA reactive and easily degraded, and **thymine** (instead of uracil) gives DNA extra stability. RNA can act as a catalyst and is thought to be the first genetic material (**RNA world**); DNA evolved from it.

**Griffith (1928) — transformation.** *Streptococcus pneumoniae*: **S strain** (smooth, with a polysaccharide capsule, virulent) and **R strain** (rough, no capsule, non-virulent). Live S → mouse dies; live R → lives; heat-killed S → lives; **heat-killed S + live R → mouse dies**, and live S bacteria are recovered. Some “transforming principle” from dead S cells had transformed R cells.

**Avery, MacLeod and McCarty (1933–44)** purified proteins, DNA and RNA from heat-killed S cells. **DNA alone** transformed R cells; **proteases** and **RNases** did not affect transformation, but **DNase** inhibited it. Conclusion: **DNA is the hereditary material**.

**Hershey and Chase (1952)** grew bacteriophages on media with radioactive **phosphorus (³²P)**, which is in DNA but not protein, or radioactive **sulphur (³⁵S)**, which is in protein but not DNA. Phages infected *E. coli*; blending removed the phage coats and centrifugation separated bacteria (pellet) from phage coats (supernatant). Bacteria infected with ³²P phages were **radioactive**; with ³⁵S phages the radioactivity stayed in the **supernatant**. So **DNA, not protein, enters the bacteria**: DNA is the genetic material.

sections.heading: 2. Structure of DNA and RNA
sections.body_md:
**Contributions:** **Friedrich Miescher (1869)** isolated an acidic substance from the nuclei of pus cells, which he called **nuclein** (DNA). **Erwin Chargaff**: in double-stranded DNA the amount of **adenine equals thymine** and **guanine equals cytosine** (A = T, G = C; A + G = T + C); the ratio (A + T)/(G + C) varies between species. **Maurice Wilkins and Rosalind Franklin** produced **X-ray diffraction** data. **James Watson and Francis Crick (1953)** proposed the **double helix** model.

**Polynucleotide chain.** A nucleotide has a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar and a phosphate. A nitrogenous base joined to the 1′ carbon of the sugar by an **N-glycosidic linkage** forms a nucleoside; a phosphate joined to the 5′-OH by a **phosphoester linkage** forms a nucleotide; nucleotides are joined by **3′–5′ phosphodiester linkages**. Purines: **adenine, guanine**; pyrimidines: **cytosine, thymine** (DNA) and **uracil** (RNA).

**Double helix:** two polynucleotide chains with a **sugar–phosphate backbone** outside and bases inside; the chains are **antiparallel** (one 5′→3′, the other 3′→5′); **A pairs with T by two hydrogen bonds**, **G with C by three**; a purine always faces a pyrimidine, giving a uniform distance between the strands; the chains are coiled in a **right-handed** fashion; **pitch 3.4 nm**, about **10 bp per turn**, **0.34 nm** between base pairs; base pairs are stacked over one another, adding stability.

**DNA vs RNA:** DNA has deoxyribose, thymine and is usually double-stranded; RNA has ribose, uracil and is usually single-stranded.

**Types of RNA:** **mRNA** (provides the template for translation), **tRNA** (brings amino acids and reads the genetic code; adapter molecule) and **rRNA** (structural and catalytic role in ribosomes).

sections.heading: 3. Packaging of DNA in eukaryotes
sections.body_md:
The distance between two consecutive base pairs is 0.34 nm, so the DNA of a typical mammalian cell (6.6 × 10⁹ bp) is about **2.2 m** long — far longer than the nucleus (about 10⁻⁶ m). It must be packaged.
- **Prokaryotes** (e.g. *E. coli*) have no defined nucleus; their negatively charged DNA is held with some **positively charged proteins** in a region called the **nucleoid**, organised in large loops.
- **Eukaryotes** have a set of positively charged basic proteins, **histones**, rich in the basic amino acids **lysine and arginine**. Eight histone molecules form a **histone octamer**. Negatively charged DNA wraps around it to form a **nucleosome**, containing about **200 bp** of DNA. Repeating nucleosomes form **chromatin**, which looks like **beads on a string** under the electron microscope; the chromatin fibre is coiled and condensed at metaphase to form **chromosomes**. Higher-level packaging requires additional proteins, the **non-histone chromosomal (NHC) proteins**.
- **Euchromatin**: loosely packed, stains light, **transcriptionally active**. **Heterochromatin**: densely packed, stains dark, **inactive**.

A unit of chromatin: about 200 bp of DNA wrapped around a histone octamer.

Densely packed, darkly stained, inactive chromatin.

sections.heading: 4. Central dogma and reverse transcription
sections.body_md:
**Francis Crick** proposed the **central dogma** of molecular biology: genetic information flows from **DNA → RNA → protein**. DNA is **replicated**; its information is **transcribed** into RNA and **translated** into protein.

In some viruses the flow of information is in the **reverse direction**, from **RNA to DNA**. **Retroviruses** (such as **HIV**) carry the enzyme **reverse transcriptase**, which makes DNA from their RNA genome; the DNA can integrate into the host genome. This **reverse transcription** is an exception to the central dogma as first stated.

key_terms.definition_md: The flow of genetic information from DNA to RNA to protein.
An enzyme of retroviruses that makes DNA from an RNA template.

sections.heading: 5. Semi-conservative DNA replication
sections.body_md:
**Watson and Crick** proposed that the two strands separate and each acts as a **template** for a new complementary strand, so each daughter molecule has **one parental (old) and one new strand**: **semi-conservative replication**.

**Meselson and Stahl (1958)**: *E. coli* grown for many generations in **¹⁵NH₄Cl** (¹⁵N, the heavy isotope, as the only nitrogen source) were transferred to **¹⁴NH₄Cl**. Samples taken at intervals were analysed by **caesium chloride (CsCl) density-gradient centrifugation**. After **one generation (about 20 min)** the DNA had a **hybrid** (intermediate) density; after **two generations (40 min)** there were **equal amounts of hybrid and light** DNA — as predicted by semi-conservative replication.

**Taylor (1958)**: using **radioactive thymidine** with root tips of ***Vicia faba*** (broad bean) and **autoradiography**, Taylor showed that DNA in **chromosomes** also replicates semi-conservatively.

**Machinery.** Replication begins at an **origin of replication**. The two strands unwind at the **replication fork**. The main enzyme is **DNA-dependent DNA polymerase**, which uses a DNA template to polymerise **deoxyribonucleotides**; deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates serve as both **substrates** and **energy source**. It polymerises only in the **5′→3′** direction, so on one template the new strand is made **continuously** (**leading strand**) and on the other **discontinuously** in short pieces (**Okazaki fragments**, **lagging strand**), which are joined by **DNA ligase**. *E. coli*, with 4.6 × 10⁶ bp, completes replication in about **18 minutes**: an average rate of about **2000 bp per second**, with high accuracy. In eukaryotes, replication takes place in the **S phase** of the cell cycle.

key_terms.definition_md: Replication in which each daughter DNA has one parental and one new strand.
Short DNA pieces made discontinuously on the lagging strand.
Y-shaped region where the parental strands separate and copying occurs.

**Common mistakes**
- Saying Griffith proved DNA is the genetic material (he showed transformation; Avery and colleagues identified DNA).
- Mixing up the labels in Hershey–Chase (³²P labels DNA; ³⁵S labels protein).

- 5-mark questions in parts: the search for the genetic material; double helix with a labelled diagram; replication with Meselson–Stahl results and the fork.

In the bacterial pellet, showing that phage DNA entered the bacteria

questions.solution_md: ³²P labels DNA, which entered the bacteria and ended up in the pellet — option (b).

Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: DNA is chemically more stable than RNA.

answer.model_answer_md: RNA has a reactive **2′-OH** group on each ribose; DNA lacks it (and has thymine instead of uracil).

questions.stem_md: State four properties that a molecule must have to act as genetic material.

answer.model_answer_md: It must be able to **generate its own replica** (replicate), be **chemically and structurally stable**, provide scope for **slow changes (mutation)** needed for evolution, and be able to **express itself** in the form of **Mendelian characters**.

questions.solution_md: Four properties.

questions.stem_md: In Griffith’s experiment, mice injected with heat-killed S bacteria and live R bacteria died. Explain this result and state the term Griffith used.

answer.model_answer_md: Some substance from the **heat-killed S** cells entered the **live R** cells and **changed them into virulent S** cells, which multiplied and killed the mouse; live S bacteria were recovered. Griffith called this change **transformation**, caused by a **“transforming principle”**.

questions.solution_md: R transformed to S.

marking_scheme.step: R cells changed to virulent S by material from dead S

questions.stem_md: Describe how Avery, MacLeod and McCarty identified the transforming principle.

answer.model_answer_md: Working between **1933 and 1944**, they **purified** the main biochemicals — **proteins, DNA and RNA** — from **heat-killed S** cells and tested which could **transform R cells** into S cells. **Only DNA** caused transformation. **Proteases** and **RNases** did **not** affect it, while **DNase inhibited** transformation. They concluded that **DNA is the hereditary material**.

questions.solution_md: Purification and enzyme tests.

marking_scheme.step: Purified components tested on R cells
DNase stopped it; protease and RNase did not

questions.stem_md: Describe the Hershey–Chase experiment and explain how its result shows that DNA is the genetic material.

answer.model_answer_md: Bacteriophages were grown on media with **radioactive phosphorus (³²P)**, labelling their **DNA**, or **radioactive sulphur (³⁵S)**, labelling their **protein**. They were allowed to infect *E. coli*; the phage coats were removed by **blending** and the bacteria separated by **centrifugation**. Bacteria infected with ³²P phages were **radioactive**, while with ³⁵S phages the radioactivity stayed in the **supernatant**. Only DNA entered the bacteria and directed new phages, so **DNA is the genetic material**.

questions.solution_md: Labels, procedure, conclusion.

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is meant by transformation? Describe Griffith’s experiment that led to its discovery. [3]
(b) A student repeats the Avery experiment but treats the S-cell extract with protease before adding it to R cells. Predict the result and explain. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Transformation** is a change in the genetic make-up of a bacterium caused by material taken up from another cell. **Griffith (1928)** injected mice with *Streptococcus pneumoniae*: **live S** (capsulated, virulent) bacteria **killed** mice; **live R** (non-capsulated) did **not**; **heat-killed S** did **not**; but **heat-killed S mixed with live R** **killed** the mice, and **live S** bacteria were recovered from them. A “transforming principle” from the dead S cells had changed R cells into S cells.

(b) **Transformation will still occur.** Protease destroys **proteins**, but the transforming principle is **DNA**, which is not affected by protease; only **DNase** would stop it.

questions.solution_md: Definition and experiment; prediction.

A stretch of B-form DNA in a double helix is 1500 base pairs long. How many complete helical turns does it contain, at about 10 base pairs per turn?
How many hydrogen bonds hold together the double-stranded DNA segment whose one strand reads 5′–GCATGC–3′?
questions.solution_md: G–C pairs: 4, each with 3 bonds; A–T pairs: 2, each with 2 bonds. Total $= 4 \times 3 + 2 \times 2 = 16$.

questions.solution_md: TAACGTG.

questions.stem_md: State Chargaff’s rules and use them to find the percentages of all four bases in double-stranded DNA with 22 percent thymine.

answer.model_answer_md: In double-stranded DNA, **A = T** and **G = C**, so purines equal pyrimidines. With T = 22: **A = 22**, **G = C = (100 − 44) ÷ 2 = 28** percent each.

questions.solution_md: Rules and values.

questions.stem_md: Name the three types of RNA and state the role of each in protein synthesis.

answer.model_answer_md: **mRNA** provides the **template** (the coded message) for translation; **tRNA** brings **amino acids** and **reads the genetic code** (adapter); **rRNA** plays a **structural and catalytic** role in **ribosomes**.

questions.solution_md: Three types and roles.

questions.stem_md: List the salient features of the Watson–Crick double helix model of DNA.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Two **polynucleotide chains** with a **sugar–phosphate backbone** outside and **bases** projecting inside.
2. The chains are **antiparallel** (5′→3′ and 3′→5′).
3. Bases pair by **hydrogen bonds**: **A–T (two)**, **G–C (three)**; a purine always faces a pyrimidine.
4. The chains coil in a **right-handed** helix with a **pitch of 3.4 nm** and about **10 bp per turn** (**0.34 nm** apart), and the stacked base pairs add stability.

questions.solution_md: Key features.

questions.stem_md: A virus genome is found to contain uracil and ribose and to be single-stranded. What is its genetic material? Give three ways in which it differs chemically or structurally from DNA, and explain why such a genome mutates faster.

answer.model_answer_md: Its genetic material is **RNA**. Differences: RNA has **ribose** (DNA has deoxyribose); **uracil** instead of thymine; and it is usually **single-stranded** (DNA double). The **2′-OH** of ribose makes RNA **chemically reactive and less stable**, so RNA viruses **mutate and evolve faster**.

questions.solution_md: RNA; three differences; stability.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Name the contributions of Miescher, Chargaff, and Wilkins and Franklin to our understanding of DNA. [2]
(b) Draw a labelled diagram of a short segment of double-stranded DNA showing complementary base pairing, the hydrogen bonds and the 5′ and 3′ ends. [2]
(c) Why are the two strands of DNA described as antiparallel? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Miescher (1869)** isolated **nuclein** (DNA) from pus cells; **Chargaff** found that **A = T and G = C** in double-stranded DNA; **Wilkins and Franklin** produced **X-ray diffraction** pictures of DNA used to build the double-helix model.

(b) **Diagram:** two strands with **sugar–phosphate backbones**; bases paired **A–T** with **two** hydrogen bonds and **G–C** with **three**; one strand labelled **5′→3′** and the other **3′→5′**.

(c) The two strands run in **opposite directions**: where one has a free **5′** phosphate end, the other has a free **3′**-OH end.

questions.solution_md: Contributions; diagram; antiparallel.

questions.stem_md: Which kind of chromatin is loosely packed, stains lightly and is transcriptionally active?
questions.solution_md: Euchromatin is loosely packed and active; heterochromatin is dense and inactive — option (c).

options.text_md: positively charged, being rich in lysine and arginine, while DNA is negatively charged
rich in sulphur-containing amino acids only

questions.stem_md: Bacterial DNA is not enclosed in a nuclear membrane. How is it organised inside the cell?

options.text_md: Wrapped around histone octamers into nucleosomes
With positively charged proteins in a region called the nucleoid, held in large loops
Dissolved freely in the cytoplasm without any proteins

questions.solution_md: Prokaryotes lack histones; their DNA is held with positively charged proteins in the nucleoid — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A stretch of eukaryotic DNA 10 000 base pairs long is packaged into chromatin. About how many nucleosomes would it form, if each holds about 200 bp?
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{10000}{200} = 50$ nucleosomes.

questions.stem_md: A bacterial chromosome has 5 × 10⁶ base pairs. With 0.34 nm between base pairs, what is its length in millimetres? (Two decimal places.)
questions.solution_md: $5 \times 10^{6} \times 0.34 \times 10^{-9}\ \text{m} = 1.7 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m} = 1.7$ mm.

questions.stem_md: What is a nucleosome? Why does a typical human cell need such packaging?

answer.model_answer_md: A **nucleosome** is a unit of chromatin in which about **200 bp** of negatively charged DNA is wrapped around a positively charged **histone octamer**. Human DNA is about **2.2 m** long in each cell, but the nucleus is only about **10⁻⁶ m** across, so the DNA must be **packed** many thousands of times.

questions.solution_md: Definition; length vs nucleus.

questions.stem_md: Describe the packaging of DNA in a eukaryotic nucleus, from the histone octamer to the chromosome.

answer.model_answer_md: Positively charged **histones**, rich in **lysine and arginine**, form an **octamer**. Negatively charged **DNA** (about **200 bp**) wraps around it to form a **nucleosome**. Repeating nucleosomes form **chromatin**, seen as **beads on a string**. The chromatin fibre is further **coiled and condensed**, with the help of **non-histone chromosomal proteins**, to form **chromosomes** at metaphase. Loosely packed **euchromatin** is active; densely packed **heterochromatin** is inactive.

questions.solution_md: Octamer to chromosome.

marking_scheme.step: Beads on a string; further coiling with NHC proteins

questions.stem_md:
(a) Calculate the length of DNA in a human cell with 6.6 × 10⁹ base pairs, and compare it with the size of the nucleus. [2]
(b) Explain how this DNA is packaged into chromosomes in eukaryotes, and how bacterial DNA differs. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Length $= 6.6 \times 10^{9} \times 0.34 \times 10^{-9}$ m $\approx$ **2.24 m**, while a nucleus is only about **10⁻⁶ m** across — so the DNA must be packed enormously.

(b) In eukaryotes, positively charged **histones** (rich in lysine and arginine) form an **octamer**; negatively charged DNA (about **200 bp**) wraps around it to form a **nucleosome**. Nucleosomes form chromatin like **beads on a string**, which is coiled further, with **non-histone chromosomal proteins**, into **chromosomes**. In **bacteria** there are **no histones**: the DNA is held with **positively charged proteins** in large loops in the **nucleoid**.

questions.solution_md: Length; packaging; bacteria.

questions.stem_md: HIV makes a DNA copy of its RNA genome inside a human cell. Which enzyme carries out this step?

questions.stem_md: State the central dogma of molecular biology and name the process by which retroviruses reverse part of it.

answer.model_answer_md: Proposed by **Crick**, the central dogma states that genetic information flows from **DNA → RNA → protein** (transcription, then translation). **Retroviruses** such as HIV use **reverse transcriptase** to make **DNA from RNA**: **reverse transcription**.

questions.stem_md: Describe the Meselson and Stahl experiment and explain how its results support semi-conservative replication.

answer.model_answer_md: *E. coli* were grown for many generations in **¹⁵NH₄Cl**, making their DNA **heavy**, then transferred to **¹⁴NH₄Cl**. DNA from samples taken each generation was separated by **CsCl density-gradient centrifugation**. After **one generation** (20 min) there was a single **hybrid** band; after **two** (40 min), **equal hybrid and light** bands. This matches **semi-conservative** replication, in which each daughter keeps **one old strand**; conservative replication would have given separate heavy and light bands in the first generation.

questions.solution_md: Method, results, reasoning.

marking_scheme.step: Results after one and two generations

questions.stem_md: Explain why one strand at a replication fork is synthesised continuously and the other discontinuously.

answer.model_answer_md: The two template strands are **antiparallel**, and **DNA polymerase** can add nucleotides **only in the 5′→3′** direction. On one template the new strand grows **towards the fork** and can be made **continuously** (**leading strand**). On the other it must grow **away from the fork**, so it is made in short pieces, **Okazaki fragments** (**lagging strand**), which are joined by **DNA ligase**.

questions.solution_md: Antiparallel; 5′→3′ only.

marking_scheme.step: Leading continuous; lagging Okazaki fragments joined by ligase

questions.stem_md: A researcher grows bean root tips for one division in a medium with radioactive thymidine, then for one division in ordinary medium, and makes autoradiographs of the chromosomes. Predict what she sees after each division and explain how this supports semi-conservative replication.

answer.model_answer_md: After the **first division** in labelled medium, **both chromatids** of each chromosome are **labelled**, because each double helix has one new, labelled strand. After the **second division** in ordinary medium, **only one chromatid** of each chromosome is labelled. Each labelled strand was kept as a **template** and paired with a new unlabelled strand, as expected for **semi-conservative** replication (Taylor’s experiment on *Vicia faba*).

questions.solution_md: Taylor’s results.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw a labelled diagram of a replication fork showing the leading strand, the lagging strand and Okazaki fragments. [2]
(b) Explain the roles of DNA polymerase and DNA ligase, and state what supplies energy for polymerisation. [2]
(c) If the E. coli chromosome of 4.6 × 10⁶ bp is replicated in 18 minutes, estimate the rate in base pairs per second. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Diagram:** parental double helix opening at the **fork**; new **leading strand** drawn continuously towards the fork (5′→3′); **lagging strand** drawn as short **Okazaki fragments** pointing away from the fork, joined by **DNA ligase**.

(b) **DNA-dependent DNA polymerase** adds **deoxyribonucleotides** complementary to the template, only in the **5′→3′** direction. **DNA ligase** **joins** the Okazaki fragments. **Deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates** act both as **substrates** and as the **energy source**.

(c) Rate $= \dfrac{4.6 \times 10^{6}}{18 \times 60} \approx$ **4259 bp per second** (about 2000 per fork, as replication is bidirectional).

questions.solution_md: Fork; enzymes; rate.

questions.passage_md:
A class repeated the Meselson–Stahl experiment on paper. Bacteria with only ¹⁵N DNA were transferred to ¹⁴N medium, and the DNA was examined after each generation.

| Generation in ¹⁴N | Heavy | Hybrid | Light |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 |
| 2 | 0 | 0.5 | 0.5 |
| 3 | ? | ? | ? |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** 0.25

**(b)** (b) Conservative replication

**(c)** (i) The **two original ¹⁵N strands** are never broken down; each stays as a **template**, paired with a new ¹⁴N strand in a **hybrid** molecule. So there are always **two hybrid molecules**, though they become a **smaller fraction** as the total doubles each generation.

**OR** (ii) Centrifugation in a **caesium chloride density gradient** separates molecules by **density**. DNA containing the heavy isotope **¹⁵N** is **denser** than DNA with ¹⁴N, so heavy, hybrid and light DNA form **separate bands**.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** $\dfrac{2}{2^{3}} = 0.25$.

**(b)** In conservative replication the parent stays heavy and the daughter is wholly light — option (b).

**(c)** (i) Original strands persist.

(ii) Density gradient.

questions.passage_md:
Two batches of bacteriophages were prepared: batch X grown with radioactive phosphorus and batch Y with radioactive sulphur. Each batch was allowed to infect E. coli for a few minutes. The cultures were then blended and centrifuged, and radioactivity was measured.

| Batch | Radioactivity in pellet (bacteria) | Radioactivity in supernatant |
|---|---|---|
| X | High | Low |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (a) DNA

**(b)** (c) To detach the phage coats from the surface of the bacteria

**(c)** (i) Radioactive **phosphorus (DNA)** entered the **bacteria**, while radioactive **sulphur (protein)** stayed **outside**. Since the material that enters directs the making of new phages, **DNA is the genetic material**, not protein.

**OR** (ii) Blending is not perfectly efficient: some **phage coats remained attached** to bacteria and were spun down with them, carrying a small amount of **³⁵S** into the pellet, though the protein did **not enter** the cells.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Phosphorus is in DNA but not in phage protein — option (a).

**(b)** Blending removed the empty phage coats attached to the bacteria — option (c).

**(c)** (i) DNA is the genetic material.

(ii) Incomplete removal.
